canonicalExplanation.summary: React Testing Library encourages tests that find elements **the way people do**. Query priority: `getByRole` with a name (`getByRole("button", { name: "Save lesson" })`), then `getByLabelText` for form fields, then `getByText` for plain content. `getByTestId` is a **last resort** for things with no accessible role or text. Interact with `userEvent` (type, click, keyboard) rather than calling handlers or setting state. Tests written this way survive refactors and also fail when a label or button name goes missing.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A lesson editor test finds the Save button with `container.querySelector(".btn-primary")`. A redesign renames the class and 40 tests fail, although nothing changed for learners. Meanwhile, a real bug, the Save button losing its text for an icon, passes every test. A save button is selected by role and accessible name rather than its CSS class. In this lesson you'll write component tests that avoid implementation-detail selectors.

```predict
{"question": "Which query would catch the icon-only Save button bug?", "options": ["getByTestId(\"save-button\")", "getByRole(\"button\", { name: \"Save lesson\" })"], "answer": 1, "why": "The role query needs an accessible name, so it fails when the name disappears. A test id doesn't care."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know the **Accessibility, errors and performance** module, the **Routing and application context** module, **Semantic and keyboard-accessible components**, and **DOM and asynchronous integration tests** (the same ideas without React).

sections.heading: The rule: query like a user, act like a user
Absent elements

includes: Query by role and name, label and text before test ids.
Interact through userEvent and assert what users see.

outcomes: Write component tests that avoid implementation-detail selectors.

examples.title: Finding the Save button like a learner
examples.situation: A save button is selected by role and accessible name rather than its CSS class.
walkthrough: **Act like a learner:** the test types into the field found by its label and clicks the button with userEvent.
**Check:** the test will survive the class rename, and it fails if the button loses its accessible name.
examples.result: Tests break when learners would notice a problem, not when styling changes.

examples.title: The test that called the handler directly
examples.situation: A test does `wrapper.props().onClick()` to "click" a button. It passes, but in the real app the button is disabled and can't be clicked.
walkthrough: Calling the handler skipped the real DOM and its disabled state.
Now the test also checks `toBeDisabled()` before the form is valid.
examples.result: The test only passes when a learner could actually click the button.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: data-testid is always the most stable and user-centered query.
misconceptions.correction: Test ids are invisible to learners and pass even when names, labels or roles break. Role, label and text queries reflect what users perceive and should come first; test ids are a last resort.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, which query would miss the missing button name?

analogy.example: Accessible queries are like **asking a friend to find "the Save button" on your screen**: they look for what's visible and named. Test ids are like **finding it by the manufacturer's serial number on the back**: stable, but it tells you nothing about whether a person can use it.
usefulFor: remembering query by what users perceive
limitations: Friends can squint; queries need exact names or regexes.
Serial numbers are fine when nothing else identifies the part.

nearTransfer.prompt: Rewrite three queries: `.title h2`, `#email-input`, `[data-testid="close"]` (an × button with aria-label="Close") using role, label and name.

farTransfer.prompt: Refactor a component test file to remove every class, id and test-id selector where an accessible query works. Note any element that had no accessible name and fix the component too.
expectedEvidence: Only role, label and text queries left, except justified ones.

remediation.explanation: For each query ask: **How would a learner find this?** Use that: role and name, label, or text. If you can't, the component may be missing an accessible name.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The test that called the handler directly".

recap.summary: To write component tests that avoid implementation-detail selectors, find elements by role and accessible name, label or visible text before test ids, interact with userEvent instead of calling handlers, use queryBy for absent elements, and assert what learners actually see.
